The Cortisol Misconception: Physiological vs. Pathological. 
You are confusing a normal metabolic adaptation with chronic, harmful psychological stress.

​When you limit carbohydrates, your blood glucose drops, and the body must manufacture its own glucose to fuel specific tissues (like the brain and red blood cells) through gluconeogenesis (creating glucose from non-carbohydrate sources like protein and fat).

Cortisol is a glucoregulatory hormone. Its job is to help mobilize stored energy. On a low-carb diet, a mild, transient elevation in cortisol can occur to signal the liver to start gluconeogenesis.

This is a controlled, systemic adaptation. It does not come with the destructive systemic inflammation, high blood pressure, and tissue breakdown seen in pathological, chronically elevated cortisol (like from severe psychological burnout or Cushing's disease). Clinical studies tracking low-carb diets show that after an initial adaptation period, cortisol levels typically stabilize, while markers of overall systemic inflammation (like C-Reactive Protein or CRP) actually plummet.

The High-Carb Reality: "Caramelizing" Your Arteries (Glycation & AGEs).
While you' re worrying about a completely natural metabolic signal (cortisol), a high-carbohydrate diet rich in glucose and fructose exposes their vascular system to a far more destructive process: Advanced Glycation End-products (AGEs). This is literally the biological equivalent of the Maillard reaction—or caramelization.
When blood sugar is chronically elevated from a high-carb diet, excess glucose and fructose float freely in the bloodstream. These sugar molecules spontaneously bond to proteins and fats in the blood and blood vessel walls without the help of an enzyme.
The structural collagen in the endothelial lining (the inner wall) of the arteries gets glycated. This forms cross-links between the protein fibers, turning flexible, elastic arteries stiff and brittle.
Fructose is up to 10 times more reactive than glucose when it comes to initiating glycation. It accelerates the formation of intracellular AGEs rapidly, driving fatty liver disease and endothelial dysfunction.
Macrophages (immune cells) have specific receptors for these warped proteins, called RAGE (Receptors for Advanced Glycation End-products). When AGEs bind to RAGE, it triggers a massive inflammatory cascade, damaging the blood vessels further and accelerating plaque buildup (atherosclerosis).

Swapping a low-carb diet for a high-carb diet to "fix" a natural metabolic cortisol spike is like burning down a house to get rid of a smoke detector. Mildly elevated cortisol for gluconeogenesis is an efficient energy-management tool; glycation from high glucose and fructose is permanent structural damage to the cardiovascular system.

You ignored the fact that this cortisol increase is safe, controlled, and necessary, while completely ignoring the massive, permanent, destructive impact that high-carb glycation and insulin spikes have on the vascular system.

​Objectively Speaking: From a strict standpoint of vascular health, tissue aging, and metabolic efficiency, the biochemical evidence heavily favors my position. The damage caused by sugar molecules binding to arterial walls (glycation) is far more dangerous and permanent than the body using cortisol to create its own clean fuel.

top_comments.text:
Dr. Chaffee,

There are two aspects of the carnivore diet that I find particularly fascinating.

First, vitamin D levels in people following carnivore or ketogenic diets often appear to be naturally higher. Given the strong association between low vitamin D status and increased all-cause mortality, that seems like an important area of discussion.

Second, I've come across studies suggesting that the type of fat consumed may influence the skin's response to UV exposure. Specifically, diets higher in polyunsaturated fats from seed oils have been associated with increased susceptibility to UV-induced skin damage, whereas diets emphasizing animal fats appear to be less prone to these effects. Since UV burns can result in DNA damage, this seems potentially significant.

I'm curious whether you think these observations are connected through metabolism, oxidative stress, or another mechanism, and whether ketosis itself may play a role in enhancing resilience to sun exposure

I just thought I'd share this because Dr. Baker was talking about marathon running and saying he wasn't completely sure how a carnivore athlete would perform at that level over long distances.

All I can do is speak from my own experience.

For people who don't know motocross, it's hard to explain just how physically demanding it really is. It's widely considered one of the toughest sports in the world because there are no breaks. No timeouts. No substitutions. No jogging down the court while the play develops. Once that gate drops, it's full intensity until the checkered flag.

Professional motocross races are 30 minutes plus 2 laps, and that doesn't sound crazy until you realize you're wrestling a 250-pound motorcycle with over 60 horsepower underneath you the entire time. Every bump, rut, braking bump, jump, landing, acceleration zone, and corner is trying to rip the bike out of your hands.

Your heart rate is through the roof the entire moto. It's common for riders to spend long periods in the 170 to 190+ BPM range while making split second decisions at high speed. One mistake can send you flying 60 feet through the air or straight into the ground. You're not just physically exhausted, you're mentally locked in every second because if your concentration slips, you're crashing.

Then add the environment. You're wearing heavy boots, knee braces, chest protectors, helmets, goggles, gloves, and full riding gear in the middle of summer. The tracks get rougher every lap. Deep ruts form. Braking bumps get bigger. The bike gets harder to control. Yet you still have to push harder because everyone around you is doing the same thing.

When I was racing at a local pro level around 19 years old, my training was absolutely insane. Marathon distances weren't some special accomplishment to us, they were just training. I would run close to 20 miles a day Monday through Friday and still do weight training on top of that just to prepare for weekend races. That was normal. You had to build an engine capable of surviving race day because motocross will expose every weakness you have physically and mentally.

Fast forward to now. I'm 31 years old and I've been retired from racing professionally for over 10 years. For a long time I stopped training completely. I got unhealthy, gained weight, my acid reflux was horrible, my energy disappeared, and honestly I felt depressed. I was just going through the motions.

Then I came across Dr. Anthony Chaffee and Dr. Shawn Baker talking about the carnivore diet. I figured I had nothing to lose, so I went all in. No cheating, no easing into it. I cut everything out and committed to giving it an honest shot.

The first few months were rough. The keto flu hit hard. But once I got through it, everything changed. The weight came off, the acid reflux disappeared, my mental clarity came back, my energy skyrocketed, and I started feeling like myself again.

Three years later I'm still carnivore. The only plant I consume is a morning coffee with a splash of heavy cream. I fast throughout the day and usually eat one large meal until I'm full.

Recently I decided to get back on a motocross bike after about five years away from riding. No training. No running. No gym. Just diet.

I expected to get completely destroyed.

The first ride definitely humbled me and I was sore, but I was shocked at how much I could actually ride. The second ride felt better. The third ride felt even better. My recovery was faster than I expected and my conditioning started coming back quickly despite doing none of the training I used to do.

That's what really got my attention.

Coming back to one of the most physically demanding sports on earth with no training and feeling the way I did has honestly made me wonder what would happen if an elite athlete trained the way I used to train while also following a carnivore diet.

Whether it's motocross, marathon running, cycling, wrestling, or any endurance sport, I genuinely believe they could be operating on another level.

Now that's just my opinion and my personal experience. I'm not claiming everyone will have the same results. But after living both lifestyles, training extremely hard while eating whatever I wanted, and now riding again while being fully carnivore, the difference has been impossible for me to ignore.

For me, it wasn't even close.

It was night and day.
